H01.reason: Devolved legislatures for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland with law-making powers; England has none, so devolution is asymmetric. The Factbook's label (parliamentary constitutional monarchy) is silent on this.
H01.citation: Scotland Act 1998; Government of Wales Act 2006; Northern Ireland Act 1998

H02.reason: Twenty regions with elected councils and constitutional legislative powers (fifteen ordinary, five with special statutes). The Factbook lists the five autonomous regions, which alone would suggest a unitary state with autonomous regions.
H02.citation: Constitution of the Italian Republic, Title V, Articles 114 to 133

H03.reason: Seventeen autonomous communities, each with its own parliament and statute of autonomy, cover the whole country. The Factbook lists them as administrative divisions.
H03.citation: Spanish Constitution of 1978, Title VIII, Articles 143 to 158

H04.reason: The Factbook's government type (presidential republic) omits the federal form; the constitution adopts it in its first article and the 23 provinces have their own constitutions.
H04.citation: Constitution of the Argentine Nation, Articles 1, 5 and 121 to 128

H05.reason: Two entities (the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska) and the Brcko District hold most powers; the Factbook labels the state a parliamentary republic.
H05.citation: Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Annex 4, General Framework Agreement for Peace, 1995), Articles I and III

H06.reason: Three directly elected members, one Bosniak and one Croat from the Federation and one Serb from Republika Srpska, chairing in rotation. An international High Representative retains powers to impose laws and remove officials (noted, not coded).
H06.citation: Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Article V; General Framework Agreement, Annex 10

H07.reason: The presidency, the House of Peoples and key offices are allocated among Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs.
H07.citation: Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Articles IV and V

H08.reason: Parliamentary seats are split equally between Christians and Muslims and allocated by sect; by the National Pact the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker a Shia Muslim. Without this field Lebanon would share an exact signature with Israel.
H08.citation: Constitution of Lebanon, Articles 24 and 95, as amended after the Taif Agreement (1989); National Pact (1943)

H09.reason: The Council of Ministers must have as many Dutch-speaking as French-speaking members, the prime minister possibly excepted.

H10.reason: Ethnic quotas for the government and the National Assembly (at most 60 per cent Hutu and 40 per cent Tutsi), carried over from the Arusha Agreement.
H10.citation: Constitution of the Republic of Burundi (2018); Arusha Peace and Reconciliation Agreement (2000)

H11.reason: The constitution gives the president no power to dismiss the prime minister, who leaves office by tendering the government's resignation, and the government is responsible to the National Assembly. V-Dem's in-practice coding (the president would succeed in removing the prime minister) reflects how presidents with a majority have obtained resignations; I follow the constitutional definition of the subtype.
H11.citation: Constitution of the French Republic (1958), Articles 8, 20 and 49 to 50; V-Dem v2exrmhgnp_5

H12.reason: Since the 2004 amendments were restored in 2014 the prime minister is appointed and dismissed by the Verkhovna Rada; the president cannot dismiss the prime minister. V-Dem's in-practice coding (0.6) leans the other way under martial law.
H12.citation: Constitution of Ukraine, Articles 85, 87, 106 and 114 to 115 (as restored in 2014)

H13.reason: The executive is the seven-member Federal Council, elected by the Federal Assembly for a fixed four-year term, collegial, and not subject to a vote of confidence. The president of the Confederation is chosen each year from among the seven and is first among equals.
H13.citation: Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation (1999), Articles 174 to 177

H14.reason: The Federal Council as a body acts as head of state and head of government.
H14.citation: Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation (1999), Articles 174 and 176

H15.reason: Two Captains Regent, elected by the Grand and General Council for six months, are joint heads of state; the Congress of State is responsible to the Council.
H15.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026), executive branch; Declaration of the Citizens' Rights and Fundamental Principles of the San Marinese Order (1974), Article 3

H16.reason: The Supreme Leader, a senior jurist chosen for life by the Assembly of Experts, is head of state, commands the armed forces and sets general policy; the Guardian Council vets candidates and legislation. The president is directly elected and heads the government.
H16.citation: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Articles 5, 57, 91 to 99 and 107 to 113; CIA World Factbook (2026): theocratic republic

H17.reason: The head of state is the Supreme Leader, not the president.
H17.citation: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Articles 107 to 113

H18.reason: The Taliban leader rules as Amir al-Mu'minin of the Islamic Emirate, a non-hereditary religious office; there is no constitution in force, no legislature and no elections.
H18.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): government type theocratic, chief of state Taliban Leader Haybatullah Akhundzada; V-Dem v16: head of state reached office by force, no legislature

H19.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026); V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 0, v2lgbicam = 0)

H21.reason: The pope, elected for life by the College of Cardinals, holds the fullness of legislative, executive and judicial power in the state.
H21.citation: Fundamental Law of Vatican City State (2023), Article 1; CIA World Factbook (2026): ecclesiastical elective monarchy, self-described as an absolute monarchy

H22.reason: Sovereignty is held by the head of the Catholic Church; laws are made by the Pontifical Commission, appointed by the pope.
H22.citation: Fundamental Law of Vatican City State (2023); CIA World Factbook (2026)

H23.reason: The pope is elected by the College of Cardinals.

H24.reason: Two co-princes, the Bishop of Urgell and the President of France, are jointly head of state with mainly formal powers; the head of government is elected by the General Council.
H24.citation: Constitution of the Principality of Andorra (1993), Articles 43 to 46 and 68

H25.citation: Constitution of the Principality of Andorra (1993), Article 43

H26.reason: Half of the 28 members are elected in two-seat parish constituencies by simple majority and half in a single national constituency by proportional representation, on separate ballots, with no compensation between the tiers. Andorra is not in V-Dem.
H26.citation: CIA World Factbook, legislative branch (2024 and 2026 editions)

H27.reason: The Yang di-Pertuan Agong is elected for five years by the Conference of Rulers from among the nine hereditary state rulers, in practice by rotation.
H27.citation: Federal Constitution of Malaysia, Articles 32 and 38 and the Third Schedule

H28.reason: The king is chosen by the nine-member Royal Council of the Throne from among male descendants of three royal lines.
H28.citation: Constitution of the Kingdom of Cambodia, Articles 13 and 14; CIA World Factbook (2026)

H29.reason: A federation of seven hereditary emirates. The Federal Supreme Council of the seven rulers is the highest authority and elects the president from among them; the Federal National Council is advisory, half indirectly elected and half appointed. V-Dem's indices (royal council, hereditary power base 0.38) would otherwise class the monarch as ceremonial.
H29.citation: Constitution of the United Arab Emirates (1971), Articles 46 to 51; CIA World Factbook (2026): federation of monarchies

H30.reason: The presidency of the federation is elected by the Federal Supreme Council.
H30.citation: Constitution of the United Arab Emirates, Article 51

H31.reason: Twenty Federal National Council members are chosen by an electoral college appointed by the rulers and twenty are appointed. V-Dem records 50 per cent of the chamber as directly elected; I treat the electoral college vote as indirect.
H31.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): 40 seats (20 indirectly elected; 20 appointed)

H32.reason: Two rival governments since 2014: the Government of National Unity in Tripoli, recognised by the UN, and a government in the east backed by the House of Representatives. No national election since 2014; the presidential election planned for 2021 was not held.
H32.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): in transition; first direct presidential election not held as planned; Libyan Political Agreement (2015)

H33.reason: The three-member Presidential Council acts as head of state.

H34.reason: The armed forces have ruled since the February 2021 coup; in July 2025 the commander-in-chief became acting president. Elections began at the end of 2025, after the V-Dem reference year.
H34.citation: V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 0, v2x_ex_military = 1.0); CIA World Factbook (2026)

H35.reason: The Sovereign Council is chaired by the commander of the Sudanese Armed Forces, at war with the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, which declared a rival administration in 2025.
H35.citation: V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 5, v2x_ex_military = 0.75); CIA World Factbook (2026)

H36.reason: The Sovereign Council is a collective head of state.

H37.reason: A nine-member Presidential Transitional Council has held presidential powers since April 2024; there has been no elected president since 2021 and no sitting parliament since January 2023.
H37.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026), executive branch note; V-Dem v16 (v2lgbicam = 0, v2expathhs = 8)

H39.reason: After the fall of the Assad government in December 2024 a five-year transition began under a constitutional declaration of March 2025, with an interim president.
H39.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): transitional presidential republic; V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 0)

H40.reason: A transitional People's Assembly was formed in 2025, two thirds chosen by indirect selection and one third appointed. V-Dem records no legislature for 2025.
H40.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): 210 seats (140 indirectly elected; 70 appointed)

H42.reason: An eight-member Presidential Leadership Council has held executive power since April 2022, while the Houthi movement controls the capital and much of the north. The House of Representatives was last elected in 2003.
H42.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): in transition, executive branch note

H44.reason: Parliament was dissolved in August 2024 after the prime minister fled, and an interim government led by a chief adviser took office pending elections.
H44.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026), executive branch note; V-Dem v16 (v2lgbicam = 0)

H45.reason: The Palestinian Authority governs parts of the West Bank under a 2003 Basic Law; Gaza has been run separately since 2007 and has been at war since 2023. The Legislative Council was dissolved in 2018 and there has been no national election since 2006. V-Dem codes the West Bank and Gaza as separate units; the scores shown are for the West Bank.
H45.citation: V-Dem v16 (units Palestine/West Bank and Palestine/Gaza); Palestinian Basic Law (2003 amended)

H46.reason: The President of the State of Palestine (also President of the Palestinian Authority) is head of state; there is no Factbook entry for Palestine as a state.
H46.citation: V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 7); Palestinian Basic Law (2003 amended)

H47.reason: Governed since 2020 by a Revitalised Transitional Government of National Unity under the 2018 peace agreement, with an appointed Transitional National Legislature; elections have been repeatedly postponed.
H47.citation: Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (2018); CIA World Factbook (2026): 550 seats, all appointed

H49.reason: The 2025 legislative election filled the National Assembly by two-round majority voting; V-Dem's share of directly elected members (12 per cent) averages the appointed transitional parliament over the year.
H49.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): 145 seats, all directly elected; V-Dem v16 v2elloelsy (2025) = 1

H50.reason: The emir suspended the National Assembly in May 2024 for up to four years.
H50.citation: V-Dem v16 (v2lgbicam = 0); CIA World Factbook (2026) gives no legislature

H51.reason: A 2024 constitutional referendum ended elections to the Shura Council; all members are appointed.
H51.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): 49 seats, all appointed; V-Dem v16 (v2lgello = 0)

H52.reason: The president heads the sole legal party, which has ruled since 1991; there have been no national elections and the 1997 constitution has never been implemented.
H52.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026), executive branch note 1; V-Dem v16 (v2lgbicam = 0)

H53.reason: The prince must sanction every law, can dissolve the Landtag and can dismiss the government; his powers were widened by referendum in 2003. Liechtenstein is not in V-Dem and the Factbook says only constitutional monarchy.
H53.citation: Constitution of the Principality of Liechtenstein (1921, as amended 2003), Articles 9, 48 and 80

H54.reason: Executive power is vested in the prince; the minister of state and the government serve under his authority and are not responsible to the National Council.
H54.citation: Constitution of the Principality of Monaco (1962), Articles 3 and 43 to 44

H55.reason: Since 2010 the prime minister is chosen by the Legislative Assembly, but the king keeps the power to withhold assent, appoints senior judges and is backed by nine seats chosen by the nobles. A borderline case.
H55.citation: Constitution of Tonga (1875, as amended 2010); CIA World Factbook (2026): constitutional monarchy, 17 people's and 9 nobles' representatives

H56.reason: The People's Consultative Assembly is made up of the House of Representatives and the weaker Regional Representative Council. V-Dem and the 2024 Factbook say bicameral; the 2026 Factbook says unicameral.
H56.citation: Constitution of Indonesia (1945, as amended), Articles 2, 19 and 22C; V-Dem v16 (v2lgbicam = 2); CIA World Factbook (2024)

H57.reason: Members are elected by list proportional representation in 18 departments, with preference votes for candidates. V-Dem's 2025 code (single transferable vote) is the only source to say so; both Factbook editions say proportional representation by party list.
H57.citation: CIA World Factbook (2024): party-list proportional representation; CIA World Factbook (2026): proportional representation

H58.reason: Most MPs are elected in multi-member group representation constituencies, where the list with most votes takes every seat; the rest are elected by first past the post. V-Dem's code for the 2025 election (two-round system) does not match either Factbook edition.
H58.citation: Parliamentary Elections Act 1954 (Singapore), group representation constituencies; CIA World Factbook (2024 and 2026): simple majority

H59.value: Parliamentary, executive president chosen by or through the legislature
H59.reason: The president is elected by Congress from among its four at-large senators and is both head of state and head of government.

H60.reason: Ten members are elected in single-seat districts by simple majority and four at large, one per state; the Factbook calls the at-large vote proportional, but with one seat per state each is a single-seat plurality race.

H61.reason: Barbados became a republic in November 2021 with a president elected by Parliament. The 2026 Factbook text still carries the phrase 'a Commonwealth realm'.
H61.citation: V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 6, legislature); CIA World Factbook (2026): parliamentary republic

H62.reason: Since the 2017 constitution took full effect in 2024 the president is elected by a 300-member electoral college and the government answers to parliament. The Factbook still says semi-presidential republic.
H62.citation: Constitution of Georgia (as amended 2017), Articles 50 and 54; V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 6); CIA World Factbook (2026): president elected by a 300-member College of Electors

H63.reason: The 2021 constitution made the president head of the executive, with a chairman of the cabinet who heads the presidential administration. The Factbook's government type (parliamentary republic) predates it.
H63.citation: Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic (2021); V-Dem v16 (v2exhoshog = 1)

H64.reason: The 2024 constitution created a president elected by parliament with mainly formal powers and a President of the Council of Ministers who leads the government. The Factbook's government type (presidential republic) predates it.
H64.citation: Constitution of the Togolese Republic (2024); V-Dem v16 (v2expathhs = 6, v2ex_hosw = 0); CIA World Factbook (2026), executive branch

H66.reason: The Faroe Islands and Greenland are self-governing parts of the Realm with their own parliaments.
H66.citation: Faroe Islands Self-Government Act (2005); Act on Greenland Self-Government (2009)

H67.reason: Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten are autonomous constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands with their own parliaments.
H67.citation: Charter for the Kingdom of the Netherlands (1954)

H68.reason: The Åland Islands have an elected parliament with legislative powers.
H68.citation: Act on the Autonomy of Åland (1991)

H69.reason: Zanzibar has its own president, government and House of Representatives within the union.
H69.citation: Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania (1977), Articles 102 to 107

H70.reason: The Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic has its own elected assembly.
H70.citation: Constitution of the Republic of Azerbaijan (1995), Articles 134 to 141

H71.reason: The Autonomous Province of Vojvodina has an elected assembly; the constitution also names Kosovo and Metohija, which Serbia does not control.
H71.citation: Constitution of the Republic of Serbia (2006), Articles 182 to 187

H72.reason: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao has its own parliament.

H73.reason: The Tobago House of Assembly is an elected assembly with its own executive council.

H74.reason: Rodrigues has an elected Regional Assembly with powers over local affairs.

H75.reason: The Factbook's two 'autonomous districts' (Abidjan and Yamoussoukro) are administrative units, not self-governing regions.

H76.reason: Sejong's 'special self-governing city' status is an administrative status, not regional autonomy.

H77.reason: Under the 2022 constitution the directly elected president appoints and dismisses the head of government. The Factbook's government type (parliamentary republic) predates it.
H77.citation: Constitution of the Tunisian Republic (2022); V-Dem v16 (v2ex_hosw = 1, v2exrmhgnp_5 = 0.6)

H78.reason: The president is directly elected, but only from candidates nominated by the House of Assembly, and a vote of no confidence forces a new election: a hybrid. I follow the Factbook's label.
H78.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): presidential republic; executive branch

H80.reason: Members of the House of the People are chosen by delegates selected by clan elders; V-Dem's last coded direct election is from 1969.
H80.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): 275 seats, all indirectly elected; V-Dem v16 (v2lgello = 0)

H81.reason: Since the 2023 coup the legislature has been replaced by appointed bodies.
H81.citation: CIA World Factbook (2026): 194 seats all appointed; V-Dem v16 (v2lgello = 0)

H82.reason: The Palestinian Legislative Council was dissolved in 2018.

H83.reason: Most members (439 of 500) are elected by open-list proportional representation in multi-member constituencies; the 61 single-member constituencies use plurality, as a list system does where only one seat is at stake. V-Dem has no code for the 2023 election; the 2026 Factbook says mixed system.
H83.citation: CIA World Factbook (2024): legislative branch; CIA World Factbook (2026): mixed system

H84.reason: Sixteen of the 24 members go to the list or candidates with most votes in a single national constituency and eight are shared by proportional representation, with no compensation between the tiers. Monaco is not in V-Dem.
H84.citation: CIA World Factbook (2024): 16 by simple majority, 8 by proportional representation

H85.reason: List proportional representation in a single constituency, with a majority bonus and a run-off between the two leading coalitions when no coalition wins a majority. San Marino is not in V-Dem.
H85.citation: CIA World Factbook (2024): list proportional representation in 2 rounds if needed; CIA World Factbook (2026): proportional representation

H86.reason: The head of the national list of the party with most votes in the general election becomes president, who heads the government and cannot be removed by a vote of confidence. V-Dem codes the route to office as the legislature; the Factbook calls Angola a presidential republic.
H86.citation: Constitution of the Republic of Angola (2010), Articles 106 and 109; CIA World Factbook (2026): presidential republic
